'''Dame Susan Jocelyn Bell Burnell''' ({{IPAc-en|b|ɜr|ˈ|n|ɛ|l}}; {{nee}} '''Bell'''; born 15 July 1943) is a Northern Irish [[Astrophysics|astrophysicist]] and [[Radio astronomy|radio astronomer]] who, while conducting research for her doctorate in 1967, discovered the first known [[Radio Pulsar|pulsar]].{{sfn|Cosmic Search Vol. 1}}{{sfn|Hargittai|2003|p=240}} This discovery was recognized by the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] in 1974, though she was not among its recipients.{{sfn|Tesh|Wade|2017|pp=31–33}}

Bell Burnell was [[president of the Royal Astronomical Society]] from 2002 to 2004, president of the [[Institute of Physics]] from October 2008 until October 2010, and interim president of the Institute following the death of her successor, [[Marshall Stoneham]], in early 2011. She was [[Chancellor (education)|Chancellor]] of the [[University of Dundee]] from 2018 to 2023.

In 2018, she was awarded the [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics#Difference between Breakthrough Prize and Special Breakthrough Prize|Special Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]]. Following the announcement of the award, she decided to use the $3&nbsp;million (£2.3&nbsp;million) prize money to establish a fund to help female, minority and refugee students to become research physicists. The fund is administered by the [[Institute of Physics#Education|Institute of Physics]].{{sfn|Sample|2018}}{{sfn|Kaplan|Farzan|2018}}{{sfn|Ghosh|2019}}{{sfn|IoP|2019}}

In 2021, Bell Burnell became the second female recipient (after [[Dorothy Hodgkin]] in 1976) of the [[Copley Medal]].{{sfn|BBC: Copley|2021}} In 2025, Bell Burnell's image was included on an [[An Post|An Post stamp]] celebrating [[women in STEM]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Cunningham |first=Paul |date=5 March 2025 |title=Special stamps launched to celebrate women in STEM |url=https://www.rte.ie/news/business/2025/0305/1500437-special-stamps-created-to-celebrate-women-in-stem/ |access-date=12 March 2025 |work=[[RTE.ie]] |language=en}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
[[File:Susan Jocelyn Bell (Burnell), 1967.jpg|thumb|right|upright|Jocelyn Bell Burnell, June 1967]]

Bell Burnell was born in [[Lurgan]], <!-- Her birth place is Lurgan, NOT Belfast. See talk page, and the sources given here. --> [[County Armagh]], Northern Ireland, to M. Allison and G. Philip Bell.{{sfn|''Lurgan Mail''|2007}}{{sfn|Bain|2022}}{{sfn|Who's Who|2017}} Their country home was called "Solitude" and she grew up there with her younger brother and two younger sisters.{{sfn|McGrayne|1993|pp=359–379}} She enjoyed her father's books on [[astronomy]], and visited the nearby Armagh Observatory, where the staff encouraged her to pursue a career in astronomy.{{sfn|Bertsch McGrayne|1998}} Her father, an architect, later helped design the [[Armagh Planetarium]].{{sfn|Johnston|2007|pp=2–3}} 

She grew up in Lurgan and attended the Preparatory Department{{efn|The Preparatory Department of [[Lurgan College]] closed in 2004,{{sfn|Lurgan College history}} the college becoming a selective grammar school for ages 14–19.}} of [[Lurgan College]] from 1948 to 1956.{{sfn|''Lurgan Mail''|2007}} At the time, boys could study technical subjects, but girls were expected to study domestic subjects such as cooking and [[cross-stitch]]ing. Bell Burnell was able to study science only after her parents and others challenged the school's policies.{{sfn|Kaufman|2016}}{{sfn|Proudfoot|2021}}<ref>{{Cite news |last=Briggs |first=Helen |date=2019-07-20 |title=Women in science: Smashing glass ceilings and glass walls |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-48953793 |access-date=2026-06-29 |work=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref>

She failed the [[eleven-plus exam]] and her parents sent her to [[The Mount School, York|The Mount School]],{{sfn|Who's Who|2017}} a [[Quaker]] girls' boarding school in [[York]], England, where she completed her secondary education in 1961.{{sfn|McGrayne|1993|pp=359–379}} There she was favourably impressed by her physics teacher, Mr. Tillott, and stated: {{blockquote|You do not have to learn lots and lots&nbsp;... of facts; you just learn a few key things, and&nbsp;... then you can apply and build and develop from those&nbsp;... He was a really good teacher and showed me, actually, how easy physics was.{{sfn|Interview at NRAO|1995}}}}

She next joined the [[University of Glasgow]], where in 1965 she graduated with a Bachelor of Science degree in Natural Philosophy (physics), with honours, and then [[Murray Edwards College|New Hall, Cambridge]], where she gained a PhD in 1969.{{sfn|Who's Who|2017}}

At Cambridge, she worked with [[Antony Hewish]] and others to construct{{efn|"... upon entering the faculty, each student was issued a set of tools: a pair of pliers, a pair of long-nose pliers, a wire cutter, and a screwdriver...", said during a public lecture in Montreal during the 40 Years of Pulsars conference, 14 August 2007}} the [[Interplanetary Scintillation Array]] just outside Cambridge to study [[quasar]]s, which had recently been discovered.{{efn|Interplanetary scintillation allows compact sources to be distinguished from extended ones.{{citation needed|date=January 2018}}}}

== Career and research ==
[[File:Chart Showing Radio Signal of First Identified Pulsar.jpg|thumb|upright|Chart on which Bell Burnell first recognised evidence of a [[pulsar]], exhibited at [[Cambridge University Library]]]]
[[File:Chandra-crab.jpg|thumb|right|Composite Optical/X-ray image of the [[Crab Nebula]], showing [[synchrotron emission]] in the surrounding [[pulsar wind nebula]], powered by injection of magnetic fields and particles from the central pulsar]]
[[File:Jocelyn Bell Burnell-1.jpg|alt=Bell Burnell attends the American Astronomical Society (AAS) meeting at Pasadena, California, 5 January 1987|thumb|Bell Burnell attends the American Astronomical Society (AAS) meeting at Pasadena, California, 5 January 1987]]

On 28 November 1967, while a postgraduate student at Cambridge, Bell Burnell detected a "bit of scruff" on her [[chart recorder|chart-recorder]] papers that tracked across the sky with the stars. The signal had been visible in data taken in August, but as the papers had to be checked by hand, it took her three months to find it.{{sfn|Schilling|2017}} She established that the signal was pulsing with great regularity, at a rate of about one pulse every one and a third seconds. Temporarily dubbed "Little Green Man 1" (LGM-1) the source (now known as [[PSR B1919+21]]) was identified after several years as a rapidly rotating [[neutron star]]. This was later documented by the BBC ''[[Horizon (UK TV series)|Horizon]]'' series.{{sfn|BBC|2010}}

She worked at the [[University of Southampton]] between 1968 and 1973, [[University College London]] from 1974 to 1982 and the [[Royal Observatory, Edinburgh|Royal Observatory]], Edinburgh (1982–1991). From 1973 to 1987 she was a tutor, consultant, examiner, and lecturer for the [[Open University]].{{sfn|Jocelyn Bell Burnell profile}} In 1986, she became the project manager for the [[James Clerk Maxwell Telescope]] on [[Mauna Kea]], Hawaii, a position she held until 1991.{{sfn|Yount|2007|p=25}}{{sfn|''Notable Women''|1997}} She was Professor of Physics at the Open University from 1991 to 2001. She was also a visiting professor at [[Princeton University]] in the United States and dean of science at the [[University of Bath]] (2001–2004),{{sfn|University of Bath|2004}} and President of the [[Royal Astronomical Society]] between 2002 and 2004.

Bell Burnell was visiting professor of astrophysics at the [[University of Oxford]], and a Fellow of [[Mansfield College, Oxford|Mansfield College]] in 2007.{{sfn|UoO|2007}} She was President of the [[Institute of Physics]] between 2008 and 2010.{{sfn|Institute of Physics: Council}} In 2013, Bell Burnell was elected Pro-Chancellor of [[Trinity College Dublin|Trinity College, Dublin]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dublin |first=Trinity College |title=Dame Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Dr Edward McParland Elected Pro-Chancellors of the University |url=https://www.tcd.ie/news_events/articles/dame-jocelyn-bell-burnell-and-dr-edward-mcparland-elected-pro-chancellors-of-the-university/ |access-date=6 March 2025 |website=www.tcd.ie |language=en}}</ref> In February 2018 she was appointed [[Chancellor (education)|Chancellor]] of the [[University of Dundee]].{{sfn|Univ of Dundee|2018}} In 2018, Bell Burnell visited [[Parkes, NSW]], to deliver the keynote [[John Bolton (astronomer)|John Bolton]] lecture at the Central West Astronomical Society (CWAS) AstroFest event.{{sfn|Warren|Thackray|2018}}{{sfn|CWAS|2018}}

In 2006, Bell Burnell chaired the 26th General Assembly of the [[International Astronomical Union]], where it was decided that:<blockquote>(1) A "planet" [1] is a [[celestial body]] that (a) is in orbit around the Sun, (b) has sufficient mass for its self-gravity to overcome rigid body forces so that it assumes a [[hydrostatic equilibrium]] (nearly round) shape, and (c) has cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit.

(2) A "[[dwarf planet]]" is a celestial body that (a) is in orbit around the Sun, (b) has sufficient mass for its self-gravity to overcome rigid body forces so that it assumes a hydrostatic equilibrium (nearly round) shape [2], (c) has not cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit, and 

(d) is not a [[Natural satellite|satellite]].

(3) All other objects [3], except satellites, orbiting the Sun shall be referred to collectively as "Small Solar-System Bodies".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2006 |title=IAU 2006 General Assembly: Result of the IAU Resolution votes |url=https://www.iau.org/IAU/Iau/News/PR2006/iau-2006-general-assembly-resolution-votes.aspx |access-date=2 November 2026 |website=iau.org}}</ref></blockquote>This led to the conclusion that [[Pluto]] would be demoted to its current status as a dwarf planet. She has spoken frequently about this decision and the public outcry which followed.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pluto - no more a planet |url=https://podcasts.ox.ac.uk/pluto-no-more-planet |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=podcasts.ox.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref>

In a 2020 lecture at [[Harvard]], she related how the media was covering the discovery of pulsars, with interviews taking a standard "disgusting" format: Hewish would be asked on the astrophysics, and she would be the "human interest" part, asked about vital statistics, how many boyfriends she had, what colour is her hair, and asked to undo some buttons for the photographs.{{sfn|Bell Burnell|2020}} The Daily Telegraph science reporter shortened "pulsating radio source" to ''pulsar''.{{sfn|Bell Burnell|2020}}

=== Nobel Prize controversy ===
Controversially, Bell did not receive recognition in the 1974 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]]. She helped build the [[Interplanetary Scintillation Array]] over two years{{sfn|''The Life Scientific''|2011}} and initially noticed the anomaly, sometimes reviewing as much as {{Convert|96|ft}} of paper data per night. Bell later said that she had to be persistent in reporting the anomaly in the face of scepticism from Hewish, who initially insisted it was due to interference and man-made. She spoke of meetings held by Hewish and Ryle to which she was not invited.{{sfn|BBC|2011a}}{{sfn|Proudfoot|2021}}

The paper announcing the discovery of pulsars had five authors. Bell's thesis supervisor [[Antony Hewish]]{{sfn|Hewish|Bell|Pilkington|Scott|1968|p=709}}{{sfn|Pilkington|Hewish|Bell|Cole|1968|p=126}} was listed first, Bell second. Hewish was awarded the Nobel Prize, along with the astronomer [[Martin Ryle]]. At the time fellow astronomer Sir [[Fred Hoyle]] criticised Bell's omission.{{sfn|Westly|2008}}{{sfn|Judson|2003}}{{sfn|McKie|2010}} In 1977, Bell Burnell commented:<blockquote>I believe it would demean Nobel Prizes if they were awarded to research students, except in very exceptional cases, and I do not believe this is one of them.{{sfn|NYAS|1977}} </blockquote>The [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]], in its press release announcing the prize,{{sfn|Nobelprize.org|1974}} cited Ryle and Hewish for their pioneering work in radio-astrophysics, with particular mention of Ryle's work on [[aperture synthesis|aperture-synthesis technique]] and Hewish's decisive role in the discovery of pulsars.

[[Feryal Özel]], an astrophysicist at the University of Arizona, characterized Bell Burnell's contributions as follows:
{{blockquote|She helped build the array she used to make the observation. She is the one who noticed it. She is the one who argued it's a real signal. When a graduate student takes that kind of lead in her project, it's hard to play it down.{{sfn|Kaplan|Farzan|2018}}}}
In later years, she opined that "the fact that I was a graduate student and a woman, together, demoted my standing in terms of receiving a Nobel prize."{{sfn|Proudfoot|2021}}  The decision continues to be [[Nobel Prize in Physics controversies|debated to this day]].

=== Honours ===
[[File:Jocelyn Bell Burnell in Manchester 2026.MP.jpg|thumb|Jocelyn Bell Burnell in Manchester, 2026]]
* In 1999, she was appointed [[Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (CBE) for services to Astronomy and promoted to [[Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (DBE) in 2007.{{sfn|Addley|2007}}
* In 2012, she was elected an Honorary Member of the [[Royal Irish Academy]] (HonMRIA).<ref>{{Cite web |date=30 April 2024 |title=Professor Susan Jocelyn Bell Burnell |url=https://www.ria.ie/members/professor-susan-jocelyn-bell-burnell/#biography |access-date=6 March 2025 |website=Royal Irish Academy |language=en}}</ref>
* In February 2013, she was assessed as one of the 100 most powerful women in the United Kingdom by ''[[Woman's Hour]]'' on [[BBC Radio 4]].{{sfn|BBC|1970}}
* She was recognized as one of the BBC's 100 women of 2014.{{sfn|BBC News|2014}}
* In February 2014, she was elected President of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]], the first woman to hold that office. She held the position from April 2014 to April 2018 when she was succeeded by Dame [[Anne Glover (biologist)|Anne Glover]].{{sfn|BBC Scotland|2014}}
* In 2016, the [[Institute of Physics]] renamed their award for early-career female physicists the [[Jocelyn Bell Burnell Medal and Prize]].{{sfn|IOP JBB Prize}}
* In 2016, she was elected an International member of the [[American Philosophical Society]].{{sfn|APS member election}}
* In 2019, she was awarded an [[Honorary Doctorate]] of Laws from the [[University of Bath]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dame Jocelyn Bell Burnell FRS:oration |url=https://www.bath.ac.uk/corporate-information/dame-jocelyn-bell-burnell-frs-oration/ |access-date=2025-09-26 |website=www.bath.ac.uk}}</ref>
* In 2020, she was elected a Legacy Fellow of the [[American Astronomical Society]].{{sfn|AAS|2020}}
* In 2020, she was elected an Honorary Fellow of the [[Learned Society of Wales]].<ref name="flsw">{{Cite web |title=Fellows: Dame Jocelyn Bell Burnell|url=https://www.learnedsociety.wales/fellow/jocelyn-bell-burnell/ |access-date=2025-09-11 |website=Learned Society of Wales}}</ref>
* A painting of her by [[Stephen Shankand]], commissioned by the [[Royal Society]], was added to the collection in the Society's [[Carlton House Terrace]] headquarters in November 2020.{{sfn|Brown|2020}}
* In 2020, she was included by the [[BBC]] in a list of seven important but little-known British female scientists.{{sfn|Shearing|2020}}
* In 2020, she was made an Honorary Fellow of [[Trinity College Dublin]].{{sfn|TCD|2020}}
* In 2022, she received the [[Matteucci Medal]] by the [[Accademia nazionale delle scienze]], Italy.{{sfn|Accademia nazionale delle scienze|2022}}
* In 2023, she was awarded the [[Royal Irish Academy]]'s [[Cunningham Medal]] and the 2022 [[Prix Jules Janssen]] from the [[Société astronomique de France]].{{sfn|RSoE|2023}}
* In 2024, she was awarded the [[Hawking Fellowship]] by the [[Cambridge Union]] in the [[University of Cambridge]].
* In the [[2025 Birthday Honours]], she was appointed to the [[Order of the Companions of Honour]].<ref>[https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/684c3e5672e2ed81c0797069/Birthday_Honours_List_2025_-_High_Awards.pdf Companion of Honour Professor Dame Susan Jocelyn Bell Burnell DBE FRS FRSE]</ref>
* In 2026, she was awarded the [[Dalton Medal]] by [[Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society]].

In 2018, she was awarded the [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics#Difference between Breakthrough Prize and Special Breakthrough Prize|Special Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]], worth three million dollars (£2.3&nbsp;million), for her discovery of radio pulsars.{{sfn|Merali|2018}} The Special Prize, in contrast to the regular annual prize, is not restricted to recent discoveries.{{sfn|Breakthrough Prize|2018}} She donated all of the money "to fund women, under-represented ethnic minority and refugee students to become physics researchers",{{sfn|Ghosh|2018}} the funds to be administered by the [[Institute of Physics]].{{sfn|Kaplan|Farzan|2018}}

Bell Burnell was the subject of the first part of the [[BBC Four]] three-part series ''[[Beautiful Minds (TV programme)|Beautiful Minds]]'', directed by Jacqui Farnham.{{sfn|BBC|2011b}}

Issued in July 2022, [[Ulster Bank]]'s new science-themed polymer £50 banknote prominently features Bell Burnell alongside other women, including those working in NI's life sciences industry.{{sfn|Friedberg|2022}} She said, "I'm passionate about encouraging more women to pursue scientific careers and I think it's something that is very important for Northern Ireland. There is a burgeoning scientific sector here. More women pursuing careers in science will support that ongoing growth."{{sfn|Bain|2022}}

=== Species named in her honour ===
A new [[nudibranch]] species {{ill|Cadlina bellburnellae|qid=Q126801013|short=yes|italic=yes}} was named in honour of Jocelyn Bell Burnell<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Korshunova |first1=Tatiana |last2=Martynov |first2=Alexander |date=6 April 2024|title=The Phyloperiodic Approach Removes the "Cryptic Species" and Puts forward Multilevel Organismal Diversity |journal=Diversity |language=en |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=220 |doi=10.3390/d16040220 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2024Diver..16..220K |issn=1424-2818}}</ref>

== Personal and non-academic life ==
Bell Burnell is house patron of Burnell House at [[Cambridge House Grammar School]] in [[Ballymena]], [[County Antrim]]. She has campaigned to improve the status and number of women in professional and academic posts in the fields of physics and astronomy.{{sfn|Bell Burnell|2004|pp=426–489}}{{sfn|Allan|2015}}

=== Quaker activities and beliefs ===
From her school days, she has been an active [[Religious Society of Friends|Quaker]] and served as [[Clerk (Quaker)|Clerk]] to the sessions of Britain Yearly Meeting in 1995, 1996 and 1997. Bell Burnell also served as Clerk of the Central Executive Committee of [[Friends World Committee for Consultation]] from 2008 to 2012. She delivered a [[Swarthmore Lecture]] under the title ''Broken for Life'',{{sfn|Burnell|1989}} at [[Britain Yearly Meeting|Yearly Meeting]] in Aberdeen on 1 August 1989, and was the plenary speaker at the US [[Friends General Conference]] Gathering in 2000.{{sfn|Taraporevala|2020}} She spoke of her personal religious history and beliefs in an interview with [[Joan Bakewell]] in 2006.{{sfn|Bakewell|2010}}

Bell Burnell served on the [[Quaker Peace and Social Witness]] [[Religious Society of Friends#testimonies|Testimonies]] Committee, which produced ''Engaging with the Quaker Testimonies: a Toolkit'' in February 2007.{{sfn|QPSW Testimonies Committee|2007|p=?}} In 2013, she gave a [[Backhouse Lecture|James Backhouse Lecture]] which was published in a book entitled ''A Quaker Astronomer Reflects: Can a Scientist Also Be Religious?'', in which Burnell reflects about how cosmological knowledge can be related to what the Bible, Quakerism or Christian faith states.{{sfn|Bell Burnell|2013b|p=11}}

=== Marriage ===
In 1968, between the discovery of the second and third pulsar, Bell became engaged to Martin Burnell and they married soon after; the couple [[divorced]] in 1993 after separating in 1989.  In a 2021 online lecture at the [[University of Bedfordshire]], Bell Burnell reflected on her first experience returning to the observatory wearing an engagement ring. Though she was proud of her ring, she said wearing it was a mistake, as, at the time, if a married woman worked it implied her husband was incapable of providing, which was shameful.{{sfn|Bell Burnell|2021}}

Her husband was a local government officer, and his career took them to various parts of Britain. She worked part-time for many years while raising their son, Gavin Burnell, who is a member of the [[condensed matter physics]] group at the [[University of Leeds]].{{sfn|Condensed Matter Physics Group|2010}}
